lessons.name: Determine the themes of short stories

textContent.text: It was another moonlit afternoon on Planet Etz, perfect for stargazing. As Rory counted shooting stars, his shape-shifter friend Zupok changed her form again and again. Rory had met Zupok when he and his family arrived here a year ago. Zupok was an alien, but she was the only one who understood how Rory felt.
Rory kicked at a moonrock with his gravity boots and sighed. "Yesterday Violet asked me to join the astro-ball team again, but I don't like playing sports. I wish she would stop asking."
"Why don't you tell her how you feel?" WHIR! Zupok's body changed from a blue butterfly to a purple flower.
Rory shook his head. "I don't share my feelings. It's not who I am."
"Says who?" Zupok asked. BANG! Zupok changed from a purple flower to a pink elephant.
Rory snapped his fingers. "You're right. Yesterday, I was a Rory who doesn't share feelings, but today I can be a Rory who does."
POP! Zupok turned herself into a big green notebook and a pencil. "Now you're speaking my language," she said with a chuckle.
Rory grinned. "Now I just need to turn myself into a writer and write down what I want to say to Violet!"

True friendship must share a common language.

textContent.text: "Poor Miss Mirela. Ever since she hurt her knee, her garden has looked a bit sad," Mama told Rolando.

Miss Mirela was Rolando's babysitter when he was little. She'd always been so lively, and Rolando still remembered how she took care of her beautiful yard. But ever since she returned from the hospital, the flowers in Miss Mirela's garden stopped blooming, and the weeds took over.
"I need to find a way to help her," Rolando thought. But he knew she took pride in taking care of her home by herself.

Rolando walked back and forth in his own yard, thinking hard about how to help. Days went by, and still he had no idea what to do. Then, one afternoon, as he watched the nurse walk toward Miss Mirela's house, an idea popped into his head.
"That's it!" Rolando said, snapping his fingers. Whenever the nurse visited, he could slip into the yard and weed the garden, knowing Miss Mirela would be too busy to notice.

Two days later, he had his chance. When the nurse went into Miss Mirela's house, Rolando sneaked into the backyard. He cleared the weeds and watered the flowers, all before the nurse left! Later that week, he saw Miss Mirela standing in her yard. Her knee looked much better.
"Look how my flowers have blossomed!" she said. "Everything seems to be growing beautifully, even without my help."
"Maybe they're growing so well because they know how much you care about them," said Rolando.
Miss Mirela smiled.

textContent.text: All through their barn chores, Bonny, Anna, and Grace chattered about tonight's harvest festival. Bonny couldn't wait to dance in the new dress Mama had sewn her.
"Aunt Harriet is sick," Mama said when they came inside. "I need one of you to take her some soup."
Bonny and her sisters frowned. Aunt Harriet lived miles away in another town. Making the trip would mean missing the dance.
"Let's draw straws," Bonny said. "Whoever gets the shortest will go."
Mama cut three straws of different lengths, then pushed them between the fingers of her fist until they looked equal in size. "Choose one," she told the girls.
"Oh no!" Bonny moaned as she drew the shortest.
Anna and Grace begged Mama to let Bonny stay. But Bonny knew her aunt needed her.
"Maybe Aunt Harriet will take you home in the wagon," Grace said, "so you can get home quicker."
Bonny thought of how kind Aunt Harriet had been to her family when Mama was sick. She'd even taught Bonny how to dance.

"No, I'll walk home," Bonny said. "Aunt Harriet needs her rest, and maybe if I dance for her, she'll feel better. There will always be another harvest. And if I'm taller by next year's dance, I can just lower the trim of my dress so it still fits!"

textContent.text: At last, it was finally Friday. Gina, Marco, and Elena always looked forward to Fridays for family movie night. Choosing a movie and ordering takeout was their favorite way to relax after a long week of middle school.
"It's my turn to pick the movie!" Gina reminded her brother and sister.
"Yeah, and it's my week to choose takeout dinner, so I'm picking pineapple pizza," Marco chimed in.
"Pineapple pizza! Ugh. I guess today's just not my day," Elena said with a sigh.
Gina and Marco exchanged a worried glance. Usually, they all looked forward to movie night, even when it wasn't their turn. If Elena was in a bad mood, it wouldn't be as much fun.
"What's wrong?" Marco asked.
"I missed all my shots at the basketball team tryouts," Elena groaned. "I just couldn't get a break!"
Gina patted Elena's arm. "Why don't you choose the movie? You've had a bad day, so you can take my turn."
"And we don't have to have pineapple pizza tonight," Marco said. "You can choose the takeout. I don't mind—as long as you don't pick anything with hot peppers!"
Slowly, Elena's face brightened. "Thanks, guys. I don't know what I'd do without you two. I guess there's always next year to make the team."

textContent.text: It was another moonlit afternoon on Planet Etz, perfect for stargazing. As Rory counted shooting stars, his shape-shifter friend Zupok changed her form again and again. Rory had met Zupok when he and his family arrived here a year ago. Zupok was an alien, but she was the only one who understood how Rory felt.
Rory kicked at a moonrock with his gravity boots and sighed. "Yesterday Violet asked me to join the astro-ball team again, but I don't like playing sports. I wish she would stop asking."
"Why don't you tell her how you feel?" WHIR! Zupok's body changed from a blue butterfly to a purple flower.
Rory shook his head. "I don't share my feelings. It's not who I am."
"Says who?" Zupok asked. BANG! Zupok changed from a purple flower to a pink elephant.
Rory snapped his fingers. "You're right. Yesterday, I was a Rory who doesn't share feelings, but today I can be a Rory who does."
POP! Zupok turned herself into a big green notebook and a pencil. "Now you're speaking my language," she said with a chuckle.
Rory grinned. "Now I just need to turn myself into a writer and write down what I want to say to Violet!"

<atomic>Rory shook his head. "I don't share my feelings. It's not who I am."</atomic>
<atomic>"Says who?" Zupok asked. BANG! Zupok changed from a purple flower to a pink elephant.</atomic>
<atomic>Rory snapped his fingers. "You're right. Yesterday, I was a Rory who doesn't share feelings, but today I can be a Rory who does."</atomic>
<atomic>POP! Zupok turned herself into a big green notebook and a pencil. "Now you're speaking my language," she said with a chuckle.</atomic>
<atomic>Rory grinned. "Now I just need to turn myself into a writer and write down what I want to say to Violet!"</atomic>

textContent.text: Candles flickered in the castle's great hall as the knights took their seats. Lady Rebecca, Chief Knight of the Ancient Order of Dragons, struck the golden orb to call the weekly meeting. She hoped for no more trouble between Lady Mabel and Lady Frida. They had been arguing about the dragons for weeks.
"The fire dragons are still attacking our water dragons. Does anyone have an answer to this problem?" Lady Rebecca asked.
Lady Mabel raised her gloved hand, and instantly, Lady Frida rose and stormed out of the room.
"One moment please," Lady Rebecca said, hurrying after Lady Frida.
"I refuse to listen to Lady Mabel ever again," Lady Frida said when Lady Rebecca caught up with her under the Great Arch."Her ideas are nonsense and I cannot agree."
"You have the right to voice your own ideas," said Lady Rebecca. "But remember that you promised to honor the dignity of all knights, and so you owe her your ear."
Lady Frida snorted and crossed her arms. But she didn't want to break the knights' code. Taking a deep breath, she returned to the hall.
"I beg your forgiveness," she said to Lady Mabel.
Immediately, whispers filled the room.
"Silence!" Lady Rebecca demanded. "Let us now hear from Lady Mabel. She has yet to share her ideas."
"I suggest a buddy system to keep watch over the water dragons," said Lady Mabel. "And I choose Lady Frida as my buddy."
Lady Frida thought for a moment, then bowed deeply before her new friend. "Your plan is as elegant as it is wise, Lady Mabel," she said. "Forgive me for doubting you."

textContent.text: Layla sat at the school lunch table, staring off into space.
"Why aren't you eating?" Omar asked.
"I'm imagining the characters for my short story. I've figured out everything I want them to do. It's going to be so perfect, the judges will be blown away!" she said.

After school, Layla wrote furiously in her notebook. The characters felt alive in her bedroom. Their voices echoed as if they were really there. "I will totally win the story contest," she thought, rereading her work.
The next day, she showed her story to Omar.

"Um…you've got a great idea…" he stammered, "but I couldn't quite see the setting. You describe it as a land of frozen ice, but none of the characters seem cold or are wearing any winter clothes. It doesn't really match."

"But they're used to being cold. They don't…" Layla hesitated. She realized that if Omar didn't understand, the judges might not either. "Actually, you might be right." Later, she made changes to her story.
When the contest results were posted, Layla ran to show Omar her prize. "The judges said my setting felt so real when they read it, they needed a hot chocolate to warm up!"

textContent.text: "Poor Miss Mirela. Ever since she hurt her knee, her garden has looked a bit sad," Mama told Rolando.

Miss Mirela was Rolando's babysitter when he was little. She'd always been so lively, and Rolando still remembered how she took care of her beautiful yard. But ever since she returned from the hospital, the flowers in Miss Mirela's garden stopped blooming, and the weeds took over.
"I need to find a way to help her," Rolando thought. But he knew she took pride in taking care of her home by herself.

Rolando walked back and forth in his own yard, thinking hard about how to help. Days went by, and still he had no idea what to do. Then, one afternoon, as he watched the nurse walk toward Miss Mirela's house, an idea popped into his head.
"That's it!" Rolando said, snapping his fingers. Whenever the nurse visited, he could slip into the yard and weed the garden, knowing Miss Mirela would be too busy to notice.

Two days later, he had his chance. When the nurse went into Miss Mirela's house, Rolando sneaked into the backyard. He cleared the weeds and watered the flowers, all before the nurse left! Later that week, he saw Miss Mirela standing in her yard. Her knee looked much better.
"Look how my flowers have blossomed!" she said. "Everything seems to be growing beautifully, even without my help."
"Maybe they're growing so well because they know how much you care about them," said Rolando.
Miss Mirela smiled.

"I need to find a way to help her," Rolando thought. But he knew she took pride in taking care of her home by herself.

Rolando walked back and forth in his own yard, thinking hard about how to help. Days went by, and still he had no idea what to do. Then, one afternoon, as he watched the nurse walk toward Miss Mirela's house, an idea popped into his head.
"That's it!" Rolando said, snapping his fingers. Whenever the nurse visited, he could slip into the yard and weed the garden, knowing Miss Mirela would be too busy to notice.

Two days later, he had his chance. When the nurse went into Miss Mirela's house, Rolando sneaked into the backyard. He cleared the weeds and watered the flowers, all before the nurse left! Later that week, he saw Miss Mirela standing in her yard. Her knee looked much better.
"Look how my flowers have blossomed!" she said. "Everything seems to be growing beautifully, even without my help."
"Maybe they're growing so well because they know how much you care about them," said Rolando.
Miss Mirela smiled.

textContent.text: All through their barn chores, Bonny, Anna, and Grace chattered about tonight's harvest festival. Bonny couldn't wait to dance in the new dress Mama had sewn her.
"Aunt Harriet is sick," Mama said when they came inside. "I need one of you to take her some soup."
Bonny and her sisters frowned. Aunt Harriet lived miles away in another town. Making the trip would mean missing the dance.
"Let's draw straws," Bonny said. "Whoever gets the shortest will go."
Mama cut three straws of different lengths, then pushed them between the fingers of her fist until they looked equal in size. "Choose one," she told the girls.
"Oh no!" Bonny moaned as she drew the shortest.
Anna and Grace begged Mama to let Bonny stay. But Bonny knew her aunt needed her.
"Maybe Aunt Harriet will take you home in the wagon," Grace said, "so you can get home quicker."
Bonny thought of how kind Aunt Harriet had been to her family when Mama was sick. She'd even taught Bonny how to dance.

"No, I'll walk home," Bonny said. "Aunt Harriet needs her rest, and maybe if I dance for her, she'll feel better. There will always be another harvest. And if I'm taller by next year's dance, I can just lower the trim of my dress so it still fits!"

textContent.text: At last, it was finally Friday. Gina, Marco, and Elena always looked forward to Fridays for family movie night. Choosing a movie and ordering takeout was their favorite way to relax after a long week of middle school.
"It's my turn to pick the movie!" Gina reminded her brother and sister.
"Yeah, and it's my week to choose takeout dinner, so I'm picking pineapple pizza," Marco chimed in.
"Pineapple pizza! Ugh. I guess today's just not my day," Elena said with a sigh.
Gina and Marco exchanged a worried glance. Usually, they all looked forward to movie night, even when it wasn't their turn. If Elena was in a bad mood, it wouldn't be as much fun.
"What's wrong?" Marco asked.
"I missed all my shots at the basketball team tryouts," Elena groaned. "I just couldn't get a break!"
Gina patted Elena's arm. "Why don't you choose the movie? You've had a bad day, so you can take my turn."
"And we don't have to have pineapple pizza tonight," Marco said. "You can choose the takeout. I don't mind—as long as you don't pick anything with hot peppers!"
Slowly, Elena's face brightened. "Thanks, guys. I don't know what I'd do without you two. I guess there's always next year to make the team."

text.text: <atomic>At last, it was finally Friday. Gina, Marco, and Elena always looked forward to Fridays for family movie night. Choosing a movie and ordering takeout was their favorite way to relax after a long week of middle school.</atomic>
<atomic>"It's my turn to pick the movie!" Gina reminded her brother and sister.</atomic>
<atomic>"Yeah, and it's my week to choose takeout dinner, so I'm picking pineapple pizza," Marco chimed in.</atomic>
<atomic>"Pineapple pizza! Ugh. I guess today's just not my day," Elena said with a sigh.</atomic>
<atomic>Gina and Marco exchanged a worried glance. Usually, they all looked forward to movie night, even when it wasn't their turn. If Elena was in a bad mood, it wouldn't be as much fun.</atomic>
<atomic>"What's wrong?" Marco asked.</atomic>
<atomic>"I missed all my shots at the basketball team tryouts," Elena groaned. "I just couldn't get a break!"</atomic>
<atomic>Gina patted Elena's arm. "Why don't you choose the movie? You've had a bad day, so you can take my turn."</atomic>
<atomic>"And we don't have to have pineapple pizza tonight," Marco said. "You can choose the takeout. I don't mind—as long as you don't pick anything with hot peppers!"</atomic>
<atomic>Slowly, Elena's face brightened. "Thanks, guys. I don't know what I'd do without you two. I guess there's always next year to make the team."</atomic>

textContent.text: It was another moonlit afternoon on Planet Etz, perfect for stargazing. As Rory counted shooting stars, his shape-shifter friend Zupok changed her form again and again. Rory had met Zupok when he and his family arrived here a year ago. Zupok was an alien, but she was the only one who understood how Rory felt.
Rory kicked at a moonrock with his gravity boots and sighed. "Yesterday Violet asked me to join the astro-ball team again, but I don't like playing sports. I wish she would stop asking."
"Why don't you tell her how you feel?" WHIR! Zupok's body changed from a blue butterfly to a purple flower.
Rory shook his head. "I don't share my feelings. It's not who I am."
"Says who?" Zupok asked. BANG! Zupok changed from a purple flower to a pink elephant.
Rory snapped his fingers. "You're right. Yesterday, I was a Rory who doesn't share feelings, but today I can be a Rory who does."
POP! Zupok turned herself into a big green notebook and a pencil. "Now you're speaking my language," she said with a chuckle.
Rory grinned. "Now I just need to turn myself into a writer and write down what I want to say to Violet!"

textContent.text: Candles flickered in the castle's great hall as the knights took their seats. Lady Rebecca, Chief Knight of the Ancient Order of Dragons, struck the golden orb to call the weekly meeting. She hoped for no more trouble between Lady Mabel and Lady Frida. They had been arguing about the dragons for weeks.
"The fire dragons are still attacking our water dragons. Does anyone have an answer to this problem?" Lady Rebecca asked.
Lady Mabel raised her gloved hand, and instantly, Lady Frida rose and stormed out of the room.
"One moment please," Lady Rebecca said, hurrying after Lady Frida.
"I refuse to listen to Lady Mabel ever again," Lady Frida said when Lady Rebecca caught up with her under the Great Arch."Her ideas are nonsense and I cannot agree."
"You have the right to voice your own ideas," said Lady Rebecca. "But remember that you promised to honor the dignity of all knights, and so you owe her your ear."
Lady Frida snorted and crossed her arms. But she didn't want to break the knights' code. Taking a deep breath, she returned to the hall.
"I beg your forgiveness," she said to Lady Mabel.
Immediately, whispers filled the room.
"Silence!" Lady Rebecca demanded. "Let us now hear from Lady Mabel. She has yet to share her ideas."
"I suggest a buddy system to keep watch over the water dragons," said Lady Mabel. "And I choose Lady Frida as my buddy."
Lady Frida thought for a moment, then bowed deeply before her new friend. "Your plan is as elegant as it is wise, Lady Mabel," she said. "Forgive me for doubting you."

textContent.text: Layla sat at the school lunch table, staring off into space.
"Why aren't you eating?" Omar asked.
"I'm imagining the characters for my short story. I've figured out everything I want them to do. It's going to be so perfect, the judges will be blown away!" she said.

After school, Layla wrote furiously in her notebook. The characters felt alive in her bedroom. Their voices echoed as if they were really there. "I will totally win the story contest," she thought, rereading her work.
The next day, she showed her story to Omar.

"Um…you've got a great idea…" he stammered, "but I couldn't quite see the setting. You describe it as a land of frozen ice, but none of the characters seem cold or are wearing any winter clothes. It doesn't really match."

"But they're used to being cold. They don't…" Layla hesitated. She realized that if Omar didn't understand, the judges might not either. "Actually, you might be right." Later, she made changes to her story.
When the contest results were posted, Layla ran to show Omar her prize. "The judges said my setting felt so real when they read it, they needed a hot chocolate to warm up!"

contents.text: My Garden

lines.text: I squint my eyes and swat at flies,
I see tomatoes red and plump.
But there's a worm that makes me squirm.
It moves, which makes me jump.
Next up I spy, roaming by,
Spiders creeping before my eyes!
Their silky threads are deadly beds
For all the buzzing flies.
I could have grown in a pest-free zone,
Chasing insects from their place.
But creepy crawlies matter, too.
They need a home, a little space.

header.text: The bolded text shows a metaphor, which compares two things without using like or as. What is the purpose of this text?

choices.text: It shows that spider webs trap the flies in the garden.
It hints that the webs will hurt new tomatoes.
It suggests that the flies and spiders work together in the garden.

contents.text: Poems don't always directly state what the author is trying to tell you. So, you often need to look closely at a poem's text to help you figure out what the poem means.

At other times, a poem might use unusual words or phrases to describe the characters or events. These uses of language are called figures of speech. Authors often use figures of speech to bring characters to life or to create a certain mood or feeling for readers.
Making inferences and understanding figures of speech can help you understand a poem's theme. The theme is the main message that an author wants you to take away from the poem.

contents.text: The Rainbow

lines.text: A rainbow stretches across the sky,
An awesome parade of colors going by.
At the top of the group is the brilliant red,
Bringing thoughts of ripe berries to my head.
Bold, bright orange brings its fiery best,
Followed by yellow, a welcome guest.
Like a wave of water come green and blue,
Flowing in with indigo and violet, too.
I see each and every single stripe.
Each one's a very special type.
But put together, they seem to shout,
"That's what teamwork's all about!"

lines.text: Ever feel a wee bit crazed,
Like a mouse caught in a maze?
Videos to watch and games to play
Keep you at your screen all day.
Stop for a moment and look around.
You'll be amazed at what you've found.
Put down your screen and you will see
All that the world contains, for free!
Take a peek at the bright blue sky.
Trace the cloud that's gliding by.
Listen to the chirping bird—
Its song just waiting to be heard.
Everything you thought you knew
Might astonish when seen anew.

contents.text: Looking Up

lines.text: Ever feel a wee bit crazed,
Like a mouse caught in a maze?
Videos to watch and games to play
Keep you at your screen all day.
Stop for a moment and look around.
You'll be amazed at what you've found.
Put down your screen and you will see
All that the world contains, for free!
Take a peek at the bright blue sky.
Trace the cloud that's gliding by.
Listen to the chirping bird—
Its song just waiting to be heard.
Everything you thought you knew
Might astonish when seen anew.

contents.text: Diamond Necklace

lines.text: In the market's parking lot
Something shines right by my spot:
I spy a diamond on a chain.
I fly off with it like a jet plane.
I explain to the store clerk, who gives a grin.
"The diamond's owner just came back in!
She left it here, and I know that she
Will thank you for your honesty."
She gushes to me just what it meant—
"The necklace was a dear present."
She presses something in my hand
A bill stares at me, crisp and grand!

contents.text: Joe's Chicken Delaware

lines.text: Joe opened up the big cookbook,
And looked for "Chicken Delaware."
He gave the recipe one quick look,
Then threw the book into the air.
The book said he must add a pinch
Of pepper to give it some zing.
But Joe dumped in at least an inch
Of pepper over the whole thing!
The steaming pan was a fine sight
That filled Joe with a great desire.
He dipped his spoon and took a bite.
His mouth and lips were set on fire!

contents.text: My Garden

lines.text: I squint my eyes and swat at flies,
I see tomatoes red and plump.
But there's a worm that makes me squirm.
It moves, which makes me jump.
Next up I spy, roaming by,
Spiders creeping before my eyes!
Their silky threads are deadly beds
For all the buzzing flies.
I could have grown in a pest-free zone,
Chasing insects from their place.
But creepy crawlies matter, too.
They need a home, a little space.

contents.text: Dripping Paint

lines.text: Drip! Drip! Watch me brush,
My painting of trees almost done.
Ring! Ring! Now watch me race.
Been waiting for an important one!
Yak! Yak! Then I hurry back.
The lines that were trees
Drizzled into streams
And decided to freeze.
I gasped a moment, then pretended
That this effect was all intended.

lessons.name: Identify supporting details in literary texts

header.text: <instructions>The following text is a conversation between Claudia and her brother Jamie. Select the best detail to show Jamie is worried about spending money.</instructions>

text.text: <atomic>"You're right," Claudia answered.</atomic>
<atomic>"A taxi is expensive. The bus is cheaper. It's only twenty cents each. We'll take the bus."</atomic>
<atomic>"Only twenty cents each. That's forty cents total. No bus. We'll walk."</atomic>
<atomic>"We'll wear out forty cents worth of shoe leather," Claudia mumbled. "You're sure we have to walk?"</atomic>
<atomic>"Positive," Jamie answered. "Which way do we go?"</atomic>

contents.text: When you make a statement about a literary text, you should include details from the text to support your statement. These details are sometimes called evidence.

header.text: For example, if you make a statement about a character's feelings, you can support it with a detail.

contents.text: <u>Statement</u>: Chad was excited for his guests to arrive at his birthday party.

sentences.text: <u>Detail</u>: "Chad couldn't sit still. He kept getting up to check for new guests."
When someone keeps checking for guests, it shows that they are probably excited. So, this detail supports the statement.
